In a flooded pearl warehouse on the outskirts of Zhuhai, China, at the hour when all legitimate commerce has ceased, a 28-year-old Chinese woman with loose waves of dark hair cascading to her waist stands with her back against a rusted diving compressor. Her pearl-beaded ivory gown, heavy with intricate beadwork catching the faint moonlight through high warehouse windows, clings wetly to her thighs where she has waded into ankle-deep seawater pooled among open oyster crates. A 32-year-old Chinese woman with a sleek low chignon polished and neat stands three paces distant, her matching pearl-beaded ivory gown similarly darkened at the hem, her arms crossed low as her gaze moves between her rival and the man who has drawn them both here. The 30-year-old Chinese man with close-cropped hair and a lean swimmer's build sits on a half-submerged crate between them, his thin white cotton shirt unbuttoned and translucent with salt moisture, skin gleaming, one bare foot dangling in the dark water. Neither woman has spoken since he pulled the first woman against him; the second watches, jaw tight, deciding whether to interrupt or offer. Pearls scatter like stars across the black water surface. Chiaroscuro light fractures through grimy windows above, catching the wet embroidery, the sheen of stretched silk, the visible tension in three throats. The camera holds them in a medium-wide tableau: two women in ceremonial gowns ruined by industrial water, one man between them with the relaxed patience of someone who has long known this moment would arrive.
